Doing The Work
DOO-ing thuh wurk
verb phrase / slogan
An activist and therapeutic catchphrase of the 2010s-2020s ('do the work' of anti-racism, of 'deconstructing' one's biases, of 'unlearning' privilege). The definite article makes it a liturgy: there is a known, ongoing, never-finished 'Work' that the conscientious must perpetually perform to be justified before the movement.

Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
A never-finished liturgy of works smuggling a rival salvation into the church; the Work that saves is finished.

Biblical Definition

Scripture sharply distinguishes two works: the finished work of Christ that saves, and the good works of the believer that flow from being saved. The first is complete and unrepeatable — on the cross the Lord cried, 'It is finished' (John 19:30); 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (Heb. 10:14). Salvation is 'not of works, lest any man should boast' (Eph. 2:9), 'not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us' (Titus 3:5). The second kind of work is real and required — believers are 'created in Christ Jesus unto good works' (Eph. 2:10) and must 'work out' their own salvation 'with fear and trembling' (Phil. 2:12) — but these are the fruit of justification, never its ground. The fatal question is always which Work justifies: Christ's finished Work, received by faith, or a Work of our own, perpetually demanded and never done.

Era

An activist-liturgy phrase ('do the work' of anti-racism, etc.) smuggling a rival salvation-by-works into the church; but the Work that saves is finished — 'It is finished' (John 19:30).

DOING THE WORK, slogan. An activist/therapeutic catchphrase for the ongoing, never-finished labor of anti-racism, bias-'unlearning,' or self-'deconstruction.'

The definite article ('the Work') marks it as a liturgy: a known, perpetual labor by which one is justified before the movement.

Structurally a rival soteriology: standing is achieved and maintained by one's own continual works, never finally complete.

Rebutted by the finished work of Christ (John 19:30; Heb. 10:14) and justification by grace through faith, not works (Eph. 2:8-9; Titus 3:5).

Key Scripture

John 19:30 — "When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost."

Ephesians 2:8-9 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Titus 3:5 — "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;"

Hebrews 10:14 — "For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."

Galatians 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Modern Corruption

An activist liturgy smuggles a rival salvation-by-works into the church: standing is earned by perpetually 'doing the Work,' a labor never finished — the exact opposite of the gospel, where the Work that saves is finished.

expand to see more

The corruption is soteriological at its root: 'the Work' is a counterfeit of justification. In the activist register, one is never righteous; one is only ever 'doing the work,' a labor of self-examination, confession of privilege, and ongoing penance that by design can never be completed — there is always more bias to 'unlearn,' more privilege to 'interrogate.' This is salvation by works in its purest form, and like every works-religion it offers no rest, only an endless ladder. Paul's verdict is total: 'by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified' (Gal. 2:16). A gospel that ends in 'it is finished' (John 19:30) and a liturgy whose whole genius is that the work is never finished are two different religions. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the activist 'Work' is named here to rebut it.

When this framework enters the church, it does not merely add an extra duty; it displaces the cross. The believer's peace rests on a Work outside himself, 'perfected for ever' by 'one offering' (Heb. 10:14); the activist's standing rests on a work inside himself, never perfected, perpetually in arrears. To import 'doing the work' as the path to acceptance — before God or before the congregation — is to set the soul back under the law that condemns, to trade the finished righteousness of Christ for the unfinished righteousness of self. It is, structurally, the Galatian error: 'having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?' (Gal. 3:3).

The recovery is the great distinction the Reformation recovered: the finished work of Christ for us, and the grateful good works of Christ in us, in that order and never reversed. We are 'created in Christ Jesus unto good works' (Eph. 2:10) — there is a real and lifelong labor of obedience, mortification, and love — but it is the fruit of a justification already complete, not the price of one still owed. The believer works hard precisely because the Work that saves him is done; he labors from rest, not for it. Christ's 'It is finished' is the only ground on which any soul may stand.

Hebrew Roots

An activist liturgy of never-finished works, a rival soteriology; Scripture answers with the finished work of Christ — 'It is finished' — and justification by grace through faith, the believer laboring from rest, not for it.

English: a 2010s-2020s activist/therapeutic catchphrase; the definite article ('the Work') makes it a perpetual liturgy.

Greek: Christ's tetelestai, 'It is finished' (John 19:30) — the saving Work completed, the opposite of an endless one.

The great distinction: Eph. 2:8-10 — saved 'not of works' (v. 9), yet 'created... unto good works' (v. 10); fruit, never ground.

Usage

"The 'Work' is by design never finished, which is precisely how you know it is not the gospel — the saving Work is finished."

"He labored to be accepted instead of from acceptance, the old Galatian error in new dress: made perfect by the flesh."

"The believer works hard because Christ's Work is done; he labors from rest, not for it."
